_doc: Stream C (owner feedback 7, V2: 'overhaul the gold rewards and item pricing'). The gold FORMULAS the rules own; js/rules/economy.js reads every number from here and tools/sim-economy.mjs (stream E) measures the result. `gear`: an item's list price = (base + perLevel x the level it was made at) x slot x rarity x extras; a merchant pays `sellFactor` of that. `kill`: what a monster pays = (base + perLevel x level) x its own weight (its Farhold `gold` / goldRef, clamped to weight[0..1]) x rank. `goldFind`: the stat multiplies KILL gold only, once, capped. Before this file a kill's gold grew exponentially with level (a level-20 brigand paid 163 gold while the average level-20 drop was priced 65), an item's price ignored its level and its slot, and quests paid less than two kills. Owner feedback 8 (W19): a backpack's price is multiplied by 1 + bagSlot x its bag slots.
_tuned: Owner feedback 7 V2, tuned by stream E (economy lead) with tools/sim-economy.mjs after C landed the formulas. Kill: 2 + 1 x level -> 4 + 1 x level, weight 0.6-1.8 -> 0.7-1.4, rank 3 / 6 / 15 -> 2.5 / 5 / 12. Gear: 45 + 42 x level -> 45 + 144 x level, sellFactor 0.04 -> 0.012. Why: with the real rank rolls (one spawn in five is a champion or a rare) and real drops (0.45 items a kill, worth two uncommon pieces on average) the first numbers paid 4.5 uncommon pieces per hour of killing at level 10; these pay about one. The whole scale is three times the first draft's so that whole-gold rounding still tells level 1 from level 2 and a 1-gold fish is small change. Only numbers changed; tests/C/playtest7 pins the rules.

retrain._doc: Owner feedback 7 follow-up: what the Unbinder charges. Farhold's shared table (68-320 gold) is a few minutes of play at these prices, so Thousandvale prices it in TIME: `hour` = an hour of questing gold at a level (base at level 1 + perLevel for each level after; fitted to tools/sim-economy.mjs: 727 / 2435 / 5610 / 10549 at levels 1 / 5 / 10 / 20), `minutes` = what taking ONE back costs in minutes of that, `allHours` = what taking everything of a kind back costs.
